blocks.text: The chapter moves from an all-encompassing announcement of judgment to a focused indictment of Judah and Jerusalem. Its sweep through humans, animals, birds, and fish is commonly understood as creation-scale imagery, evoking reversal and flood-like devastation. The specific charges that follow include Baal worship, worship of the heavenly host from rooftops, divided oath-taking, turning away, and failing to seek Jehovah. The chapter closes by portraying the near “day of Jehovah” through battle alarm, darkness, distress, ruined defenses, and wealth that cannot rescue its owners. Scholars also disagree about how the book’s larger parts were composed and related, as well as its precise dating in relation to Josiah’s reign.

The judgment is described within the city as well as on a cosmic scale. The Fish Gate, the Second Quarter, the hills, and Maktesh mark Jerusalem as the setting for cries and economic collapse, although their exact archaeological locations remain uncertain. The silence and sacrifice imagery in verses 7–9 introduces a scene in which Jehovah prepares a sacrifice and consecrates guests before naming officials, royal sons, foreign dress, threshold behavior, violence, and fraud as targets. The lamp-lit search in verses 12–13 exposes residents settled in complacency who assume that Jehovah will neither act for good nor for evil; their houses, vineyards, and wealth are then turned into losses. The long genealogy in verse 1 does not securely establish either African ancestry through Cushi or royal descent through Hezekiah.

Verse 1 identifies Zephaniah through four generations and places the message during Josiah’s reign. The book has also been preserved in several textual witnesses, including the Masoretic text, the Old Greek translation, Judean Desert manuscripts, later interpretive commentaries, and other versions. Their differences in several difficult passages are a reminder that the text has a long and complex history of transmission.
